title: Ash chopping board
subtitle: An end-grain board for the kitchen counter
excerpt: An end-grain chopping board in seasoned ash: 30 cm by 22 cm, 4 cm thick. End-grain boards are gentler on knife edges than long-grain boards and self-heal light cuts. Finished with board butter; no glue joints at this scale.
sourceNotes: Traditional British kitchen-craft pattern; end-grain board construction documented in Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics (1885) under household woodwork.

glossaryTerms.definition: The face of a board exposed when timber is cut across the grain. End-grain surfaces are harder-wearing as a cutting surface than long-grain and close up lightly after knife use.
Timber dried to equilibrium moisture content (8 to 12 per cent for indoor use). Dimensionally stable; does not shrink significantly after working.

content.text: An
end-grain
chopping board in
seasoned wood

ash. The board is cut from a single piece of timber with the saw running across the grain, leaving the growth rings standing vertically on the top face. At this scale, no glue joints are needed. Food-safe board butter is the finish; reapply monthly.
Wood

Seasoned ash: a piece 22 cm wide, 4 cm thick, and 30 cm long cut from flat-sawn board stock. Ash is open-grained but hard enough for a kitchen board; beech is the traditional British chopping-board timber and works identically. Avoid softwoods (pine, spruce) for a cutting surface: they compress and score too easily. The timber must be kiln-dried or air-dried to 8 to 12 per cent moisture content; green timber will crack as it dries after finishing.
Tools
Tenon saw: for the cross-grain cut.
Marking gauge: to score the cut line.
Try square, 200 mm: to check the face is square.
Sanding block with 120-grit, then 240-grit, then 320-grit paper: for the faces and edges.
Card scraper (optional): for a glass-smooth face without sanding marks.
Board butter: beeswax-and-mineral-oil paste, food-safe finish.
Method
Step 1: Mark and saw the board

Mark the 30 cm length across the face and edges of the board with the marking gauge and try square. Saw on the waste side of the line with the tenon saw, keeping the cut vertical. Check the end face with the try square: it should be square to both the face and edge. If the saw cut wandered, a plane or sanding block on the end face corrects it.
Step 2: Sand the top face

Start with 120-grit on the sanding block. Work across the face in the grain direction. The end-grain face will sand evenly but is slightly harder than the side-grain edges. Move to 240-grit and then 320-grit. The surface should be smooth to the touch and free of saw marks. A card scraper, if you have one, produces a finer surface than sanding and leaves no paper residue in the open pores of the ash.
Step 3: Round the edges
Use 120-grit paper to break the sharp arris on all four long edges and both end faces. A sharp corner on a kitchen board chips off in use. Work through to 240-grit on the edges.
Finishing

Apply board butter generously to all surfaces with a cloth or your fingers. Work it into the end-grain face, which is more absorbent than the side grain. Leave for ten minutes, then wipe off the surplus with a dry cloth. The board is ready to use once dry (about one hour). Re-apply monthly, or whenever the wood looks dry.
Variations
Beech: the standard British chopping-board wood. Closer grain than ash; takes the sanded finish slightly smoother.
Smaller bread board: 20 cm by 15 cm, 2.5 cm thick. Same method; lighter to lift.
Feet: four rubber feet screwed to the underside stop the board sliding. Pre-drill and counter-sink the screw holes before finishing.
Care

Wash by hand with hot soapy water. Dry with a cloth immediately; never leave standing in water or put in a dishwasher. Re-oil with board butter monthly. A board that has developed deep cuts can be sanded back to a fresh surface: work through the grits again and re-oil.

attrs.symptom: The end face is not square
attrs.cause: The tenon saw wandered during the cut.
attrs.fix: Clamp the board and work down the face with a sanding block on a flat surface, keeping the block vertical. Check frequently with the try square.

attrs.symptom: The surface is rough after sanding
attrs.cause: Too much pressure on the sanding block, or skipping grits.
attrs.fix: Work through the grits in order: 120, 240, 320. Light pressure; let the abrasive do the work. The end-grain face needs more passes than the long-grain edges.

attrs.symptom: The board is lifting or warping after a few weeks
attrs.cause: The timber was not fully seasoned, or only one face was oiled.
attrs.fix: Oil all six faces equally, including the bottom. Uneven finishing causes uneven moisture absorption and can pull the board into a curve.
